strengths: Integrating label propagation and label spreading into BORE-style optimization is a simple, potentially useful contribution, especially when candidate pools are already available. The paper explains both transductive prediction and an inductive extension for continuous search.

The experiments compare against GP-EI/UCB and multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers across synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and MNIST. Twenty repeated runs with standard errors and substantial improvements in several settings provide meaningful evidence of practical promise.

The appendices investigate bandwidth, threshold ratios, unlabeled sampling, and pool subsampling, including a no-transduction control. Pseudocode, search-space descriptions, and model architectures aid understanding, and the paper acknowledges computational and theoretical limitations.
weaknesses: The central explanation for improved exploration is insufficiently supported. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure that density clusters align with objective-threshold labels, as Assumption 4.1 requires. Appendix C does not establish the claimed decision-set expansion or connect it to optimization performance; it explicitly acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. semi-supervised learning results do not apply to adaptive BO. A broader positive region alone does not demonstrate a better exploration–exploitation balance.

The headline gains are not convincingly attributed to unlabeled data. Figure 12 includes a useful no-transduction control, but fixes beta at 0.5 while the main experiments learn beta. The control actually performs better in several cases, including Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. Matched, appropriately tuned kernel-classifier controls and ablations of randomized tie handling are needed to distinguish the benefits of label propagation from bandwidth selection and acquisition-search heuristics. This matters because the principal novelty is the integration of established components.

The 64D MNIST experiment offers limited evidence for general high-dimensional black-box optimization. Appendix D.5 constructs its representation using a classifier trained on 440,000 labeled examples of the exact three-digit number subsequently minimized. This supplies substantial task-specific supervision and favorable representation structure. A baseline that ranks candidates using the pretrained classifier, and evaluation with representations learned without objective labels, would clarify what the optimizer contributes.

Important implementation and comparison details remain unclear. The paper specifies L-BFGS-B acquisition maximization without adequately explaining selection from arbitrary fixed pools or how baseline acquisitions are optimized. Whether randomized tie handling is shared with the baselines is also unspecified, which matters for piecewise-constant tree classifiers. Input scaling, beta optimization bounds and initialization, and propagation hyperparameters are insufficiently documented despite their direct influence on the graph geometry and results.

The practical scope and computational tradeoffs need stronger evaluation. Continuous-search experiments cover only four two-dimensional functions. Dense graph construction scales quadratically with the number of points, while the main method repeatedly learns beta and uses 1,000 acquisition-optimization starts. Figure 8 compares subset sizes under fixed beta rather than reporting comparative runtime for the complete methods, leaving their practical efficiency uncertain.

A correctable mathematical inconsistency affects reproducibility: the entrywise transition definition in Section 4.1 implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W and Equation (7) subsequently uses P transposed. The normalization convention and implemented update should be reconciled.
